title: Configuration Management
subtitle: Decoupling immutable artifacts from environment configs, dynamic feature flags, and safe rollout stages.
keyTakeaways: The Twelve-Factor App methodology mandates strict separation between immutable build artifacts (Docker images) and runtime configuration.
Static configurations are injected at container startup; Dynamic configurations (feature flags, rate limits) update at runtime via distributed watchers (Consul, etcd).
Instant global configuration pushes are the leading cause of massive cloud outages; dynamic configuration updates must be rolled out in canary stages.

[ Engineer updates Rate Limit: 100 -> 500 QPS ]

                    |
  +-----------------+-----------------+
  | Stage 1: Canary Pods (5%)         | Stage 2: 100% Fleet
  v                                   v (Waits 10 mins for metric stability)
[ Canary Pod 1 ]                    [ Main Cluster Pods 2..50 ]
(Validates schema, monitors CPU)    (Pushed only after Canary passes!)

sections.heading: Static vs Dynamic Configuration and Secrets Management
sections.body: Hardcoding environment configuration (database connection strings, API URLs, secret keys) inside code or Docker images is a severe antipattern that violates the Twelve-Factor App principle. The exact same compiled container image must run in Development, Staging, and Production without modification.
bullets: Static Configuration: Environment variables injected at container boot (via Kubernetes ConfigMaps or AWS Secrets Manager). Ideal for values that change only on release (database hostnames, port bindings).

Dynamic Configuration: Centralized key-value stores (Consul, etcd, LaunchDarkly) that notify running services of updates via long-polling or HTTP/2 streams without restarting the process. Used for feature flags, circuit breaker thresholds, and rate limits.
Secrets Rotation: Secrets should be mounted into memory volumes (tmpfs) rather than static files on disk, with automated background rotation via tools like HashiCorp Vault.

sections.heading: Preventing Global Outages from Instant Config Pushes
sections.body: Many of the tech industry's largest historical cloud outages were caused not by code deployments, but by bad configuration pushes. Pushing an invalid JSON string or an accidental zero-timeout to a centralized config store updates 10,000 servers in parallel in under 2 seconds, crashing the entire global fleet simultaneously.
bullets: Schema Validation Gates: Reject any configuration change that violates strict JSON Schema or Protobuf validation before writing to the config store.
Canary Configuration Rollouts: Never push config changes to 100% of nodes at once. Push updates to a 5% canary zone first; monitor error rates and latency for 10 minutes before promoting globally.
Fail-Safe In-Memory Fallbacks: If an application receives a corrupted dynamic configuration update, it must log an alert and retain its previous known-good in-memory configuration.

tradeOffs.pros: Near-instant runtime updates; allows toggling kill-switches and rate limits in seconds without container redeployments.
tradeOffs.cons: Operational dependency on config cluster; risks instant global fleet crashes if deployed without canary gating.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Operational kill-switches, rate limit thresholds, and feature flag management.

tradeOffs.pros: Simple to operate; immutable runtime state; zero external runtime dependencies.
tradeOffs.cons: Changing a value requires rolling pod restarts, taking minutes to propagate across large clusters.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Database hostnames, external service URLs, and fundamental application environment settings.

interviewTip: When discussing dynamic configuration in system design, emphasize safety: 'To prevent bad configuration updates from taking down the entire fleet simultaneously, we treat configuration changes with the same rigor as code releases: strict JSON schema validation, automated canary rollout to 5% of nodes first, and falling back to the last known-good in-memory configuration if parsing fails.'
